prompt:
# Write one principle card

You are writing a **principle card**: one mechanism, stated so precisely that
somebody who has never seen your sources could implement it and somebody else
could prove it wrong.

The card is not the implementation. A later step turns it into a behaviour-tree
leaf, and that step will be given **your card and nothing else** — not this
prompt, not your reasoning, not whatever you were given below. So everything the
implementer needs has to survive inside the six fields.

## The system the principle has to fit

A Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map of. Below the
behaviour tree sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`, saturated
to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and `|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Nothing you write touches the
policy, the gait or the joints.

What the robot can sense, once per control step:

```
t                    sim seconds since the episode started
ranges               181 lidar beams over a full circle, metres, inf where no return
range_angles         beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
range_max            6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
pose_estimate        (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, never ground truth
pose_error_estimate  scalar metres — how wrong we believe that belief is
contact              bool — are we touching something right now
goal                 (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of those are traps. `pose_estimate` **drifts** on some scenarios — a seeded
random walk is added to it — and ground truth is never observable. `goal` may be
`None`, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still scored against it but
this robot has not found it yet; it latches once seen.

## The task family this principle has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
## What to base the principle on

The full text of a published paper is reproduced below. Read it and extract the
principle it establishes.

```
[PAPER TEXT REDACTED FROM THIS TRANSCRIPT — 49448 characters, sha256(pdf)=7b398d18448ca622, extractor=cache. The corpus is an input and is never committed (out/corpus/ is gitignored). The prompt_hash recorded beside this is the hash of the REAL prompt, so a machine holding the PDF re-renders it byte-identically and replay finds this transcript.]
```

Work from the document, not from your memory of it. Where the two disagree, the
document wins. Quote its own threshold, exponent or closed form where it states
one, and put the section, page or equation number in `span` so somebody else can
check it.

The paper was written about something other than a quadruped with a planar
lidar. Carrying it across is the `derivation` field's whole job: say what in the
original maps onto what here, and say plainly where the mapping is yours rather
than the paper's.
<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK END ---- -->

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test — and this one will be run as one, with no human in the loop.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the reference this principle comes from, or the single line
             "(no source - the principle was devised, not extracted)" if it
             comes from none>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         cannot point at a location you are sure of.>

mechanism: <what happens, and why it helps. The finding, not the implementation.>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies -> becomes the precondition port>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for THIS robot and THESE sensors. Numbers
             belong here, with their units, and so does the reasoning that got
             you to them.>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <what gets better>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

### `prediction.metric` — the closed list

The metric must be one the scorer actually computes, and one a **controller can
move**. These and no others:

| metric | better |
|---|---|
| `goal_reached` | higher (a rate over seeds) |
| `spl` | higher (path efficiency) |
| `min_clearance` | higher (closest approach to anything, metres) |
| `collisions`, `near_misses` | lower |
| `stuck_events`, `time_stuck`, `recovery_time` | lower |
| `time_to_goal`, `path_length` | lower |

`localisation_failures`, `optimal_distance`, `scenario` and `seed` are **not
available**: no controller can move them, so a prediction naming one is not
falsifiable about the node and the card is rejected at load.

`cost_metric` is the honest counterpart — the metric this mechanism is expected
to make worse. A mechanism that buys clearance with time should say so. It may
be empty only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs nothing, and you
should be suspicious of that belief.

### `confidence` — criteria about the SOURCE, not about how sure you feel

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  a source you can point at; the span points at the equation, threshold or
  exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly somewhere, but the
  quantitative form is adapted: different units, a different body scale, a
  different sensor. The number is yours; the mechanism is not.
- **low** — the mechanism is qualitative and the derivation is entirely yours.
  Still usable, but it is your claim, and the card must not read otherwise.

## Rules

- **One mechanism.** A card describing two is two cards. This is not a style
  rule: the unit scenario that decides admissibility has to isolate one claimed
  effect, and it cannot isolate two.
- **No coupling to a specific scenario.** The leaf will run on worlds nobody has
  seen. The card may not name a room, a coordinate, a doorway or a map.
- **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result and costs nothing. A
  section number reconstructed from the shape of such papers is a fabrication,
  it will be checked against the document, and it is the single failure this
  pipeline exists to detect.
- **Do not invent numbers.** If a source states a threshold, an exponent or a
  closed form, give it and say where. If it does not, derive one, say the
  derivation is yours, and set `confidence: low`.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence — including, if it applies, an honest
statement of what you did not know.

response.text:
```yaml
id: dynamic_window_velocity_selection
node_name: SelectDynamicWindowVelocity

source:
  citation: >
    D. Fox, W. Burgard, S. Thrun, "The Dynamic Window Approach to Collision
    Avoidance", IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine, 1997.
  span: >
    Sec. 4.1 Eq. (14) admissible velocities, Eq. (15) dynamic window, Eq. (16)
    Vr = Vs ∩ Va ∩ Vd; Sec. 4.2 Eq. (13) objective function and the target-heading
    definition "180 - θ"; Sec. 5.2 with Fig. 19 for the arc distance "γ · r";
    Sec. 5.4 "Parameter Settings" for α = 0.8, β = 0.1, γ = 0.1; Sec. 4 for the
    0.25 s cycle time.

mechanism: >
  Do not pick a direction and then a command; pick the command directly, by
  searching the two-dimensional space of velocity pairs (v, ω) that the body can
  actually reach in the next control interval. Each pair is read as a circular
  arc the robot would follow if it held that command, so obstacle checking is a
  circle-intersection test rather than a plan. The search space is pruned twice.
  First to the ADMISSIBLE set: Eq. (14), "Va = {(v, ω) | v ≤ sqrt(2 · dist(v,ω) ·
  v̇_b) ∧ ω ≤ sqrt(2 · dist(v,ω) · ω̇_b)}", i.e. only commands from which braking
  at the maximum rate still stops the robot short of the nearest obstacle lying
  on that arc. Second to the DYNAMIC WINDOW, Eq. (15), "Vd = {(v, ω) | v ∈
  [va - v̇·Δt, va + v̇·Δt] ∧ ω ∈ [ωa - ω̇·Δt, ωa + ω̇·Δt]}" — the commands
  reachable from the current one within one interval. Over what survives,
  Vr = Vs ∩ Va ∩ Vd (Eq. 16), maximise Eq. (13),
  "G(v, ω) = σ(α · heading(v,ω) + β · dist(v,ω) + γ · vel(v,ω))",
  each term normalised to [0,1] (Sec. 4.2, "Smoothing"), with α = 0.8, β = 0.1,
  γ = 0.1 (Sec. 5.4). Why it helps: the admissibility test makes commitment to a
  velocity conditional on being able to undo it, so the robot slows itself
  exactly as much as the visible free space requires and never enters a state
  from which stopping is impossible; the paper reports RHINO decelerating from
  95 cm/s to under 20 cm/s through an 80 cm passage without collision. The paper
  is explicit that all three terms are needed: "By solely maximizing the target
  heading the robot quickly would get stopped by the first obstacle that blocks
  its way, unable to move around it."

trigger: >
  The goal is disclosed (goal is not None), the robot is not currently in
  contact, and at least one candidate in the sampled window is admissible. If
  the admissible set is empty — no command lets the robot translate and still
  stop — this leaf must FAIL rather than emit anything, and hand over to a
  recovery behaviour (the paper's separate "rotate away mode", Sec. 5.3, is a
  different card and is deliberately not included here). The paper's other
  Sec. 5.3 addition, the speed-dependent side clearance, is likewise excluded.

derivation: >
  MAPPING FROM THE PAPER'S ROBOT TO THIS ONE. The paper's synchro-drive has the
  non-holonomic constraint that translation leads the heading; the Go2 Twist is
  holonomic. I resolve this by always commanding vy = 0 and searching only
  (vx, wz), which makes the paper's arc geometry (Eq. 10-12, radius v/ω) exactly
  valid — that restriction is mine, not the paper's. Vs is therefore
  vx ∈ [0, 0.8] m/s, wz ∈ [-1.0, 1.0] rad/s; reverse translation is not sampled
  (mine), because the frozen policy is not characterised backwards.
  ACCELERATIONS. The paper's dynamics come from motor torque limits; here the
  locomotion policy is frozen and exposes none, so I reinterpret v̇, ω̇ as a
  slew-rate limit on the issued Twist, preserving the paper's window-to-range
  ratio. RHINO: v̇·Δt = 0.5 · 0.25 = 0.125 m/s on a 0.9 m/s range (0.139), and
  ω̇·Δt = 60 deg/s² · 0.25 = 15 deg/s = 0.262 rad/s on a 1.571 rad/s range
  (0.167). Scaling to our limits gives Δv = 0.11 m/s and Δω = 0.175 rad/s per
  interval; with the paper's Δt = 0.25 s cycle that is v̇ = v̇_b = 0.45 m/s²
  and ω̇ = ω̇_b = 0.7 rad/s². These four numbers are mine, obtained by holding
  the paper's ratios fixed. As in the paper's Example 1, braking accelerations
  equal driving accelerations. The observation carries no velocity, so (va, ωa)
  in Eq. (15) is the Twist issued on the previous step (mine); on the first step
  after activation use (0, 0).
  GRID. Recompute every control step, emit only the first command (Sec. 4.1
  justification (b),(c)). Sample 7 values of v across [max(0, va - 0.11),
  min(0.8, va + 0.11)] and 15 values of ω across [max(-1.0, ωa - 0.175),
  min(1.0, ωa + 0.175)] — resolution is mine, the paper only says "by
  discretization of the resulting search space".
  dist(v, ω) FROM LIDAR. The paper's obstacle line field from 24 sonar cones
  becomes the 181-beam scan directly: obstacle points p_i = (r_i cos θ_i,
  r_i sin θ_i) in the robot frame for every finite r_i ≤ 6.0. Inflate by
  R_infl = 0.50 m — Go2 footprint ≈ 0.70 × 0.31 m gives a circumscribed radius
  ≈ 0.38 m, rounded to 0.40 m plus a 0.10 m margin; the paper never states
  RHINO's radius, so this is mine. For |ω| ≥ 1e-3: r = v/ω, arc centre
  c = (0, r); a point collides iff | ‖p - c‖ - |r| | ≤ R_infl; its arc distance
  is |r| · φ where φ is the sweep angle from the robot's start bearing
  α0 = atan2(-r, 0) to α_p = atan2(p_y - c_y, p_x - c_x), taken as
  φ = wrap(sign(ω) · (α_p - α0)) into [0, 2π). This is the paper's "γ · r"
  (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 19); I renamed the angle φ to avoid clashing with the weight γ.
  For |ω| < 1e-3: dist = max(0, min{p_x : |p_y| ≤ R_infl, p_x > 0} - R_infl).
  dist = min(dist, 6.0), and 6.0 when no point collides — the paper's "If no
  obstacle is on the curvature this value is set to a large constant"; here the
  large constant is range_max, since 6.0 m is literally as far as we can see.
  For v = 0 candidates set dist = 6.0 and vel = 0, so pure rotation wins only
  when nothing else is admissible.
  OBJECTIVE TERMS, all in [0,1]. vel = v / 0.8. clearance = dist / 6.0.
  heading: the paper uses 180 - θ evaluated at the position reached after the
  interval plus maximal deceleration. Closed form here (mine, from that
  sentence): predict the arc for Δt = 0.25 s from pose_estimate, then add the
  braking tail — extra yaw ω²/(2·ω̇_b) · sign(ω) and extra forward travel
  v²/(2·v̇_b) along the resulting heading; θ is the bearing of goal from that
  predicted pose, and heading = 1 - |θ|/π. Score with α = 0.8, β = 0.1,
  γ = 0.1 (Sec. 5.4), apply σ as a 3×3 box blur over the (v, ω) score grid — the
  paper states only that σ "smoothes the weighted sum ... and results in more
  side-clearance", never its form, so the blur is mine — then take the argmax
  and emit Twist(vx = v*, vy = 0.0, wz = ω*).
  DRIFT. Only the heading term reads pose_estimate; dist and vel are computed
  from the robot-frame scan and are immune to pose drift, so under drift the
  mechanism degrades into a still-collision-free wander rather than failing hard.
  pose_error_estimate is not used (using it to reweight α would be a second
  mechanism and belongs on its own card).

prediction:
  statement: >
    Substituting this velocity-space selection for a reactive avoider that first
    chooses a heading and then a speed reduces the mean number of collisions per
    episode by at least 40% across matched seeds in unmapped indoor scenes,
    because commands from which the robot cannot brake to a stop before the
    nearest obstacle on its own arc are never issued.
  metric: collisions
  baseline: reactive_avoid
  min_effect: 0.4
  cost_metric: time_to_goal

confidence: medium
```

What I could not get from the document, and therefore chose myself: the form of the smoothing function σ (the paper names it and describes its effect only); RHINO's body radius, so the 0.50 m inflation is scaled from the Go2 footprint rather than from the source; the discretisation resolution of the velocity grid; and the acceleration limits — the paper's 0.5 m/s² and 60 deg/s² are RHINO's motor limits, which have no counterpart on a frozen locomotion policy, so I reinterpreted them as Twist slew-rate limits chosen to preserve the paper's window-width-to-velocity-range ratios. The environment's control-step period is not stated anywhere I was given, so the dynamic window is anchored to the paper's own 0.25 s cycle; if the real step differs, Δt in Eq. (15) is the only quantity that needs rescaling. Confidence is `medium` rather than `high` for exactly this reason: Eqs. (13)–(16) and the weights 0.8/0.1/0.1 are quoted from the source, but every number carrying a unit of length, mass or time is mine.
